madrid.name: Madrid
madrid.blurb: Spain's capital. Big-city density, late dinners, world-class museums. Expensive by Spanish standards but cheap by NYC/SF standards. The expat scene is concentrated around Salamanca and Chamberí; the up-and-coming American clusters are in Lavapiés and La Latina.
madrid.weather: continental — hot dry summers (35–40°C), crisp dry winters (occasional snow)
madrid.best_neighborhoods: Chamberí (residential, walkable), Salamanca (upscale), Lavapiés (artsy, diverse), Malasaña (nightlife)
madrid.expat_density: high — largest English-speaking community in Spain
madrid.pros: best public transport in Spain, biggest job market, most international, English widely spoken in tourism/finance
madrid.cons: rent has spiked 15-20% YoY since 2023, no beach, summer is brutal
madrid.consulate_route: Houston / NYC / Chicago / SF / LA / Miami — Houston is the fastest as of early 2026

barcelona.name: Barcelona
barcelona.blurb: Beach, mountains, Gaudí, and a tech scene that grew faster than the housing supply. Catalonia operates with its own rhythm and language; Spanish works fine but Catalan is everywhere. Tighter rental market than Madrid.
barcelona.weather: Mediterranean — mild winters (10–15°C), warm summers (28–32°C), high humidity in August
barcelona.best_neighborhoods: Eixample (central, grid-pattern, expensive), Gràcia (village feel, cheaper), Poblenou (tech corridor, ex-industrial), El Born (touristy but charming)
barcelona.expat_density: very high — major tech and digital nomad hub
barcelona.pros: beach + mountains in 30 min, biggest startup scene in Spain, walkable everywhere, direct flights to most of Europe
barcelona.cons: tightest rental market in Spain, anti-tourist sentiment in some neighborhoods, Catalan administrative friction
barcelona.consulate_route: any US consulate, but BCN-bound applicants often use NYC or Houston

valencia.name: Valencia
valencia.blurb: The quiet winner of the Spain expat boom. Beach, the Turia park (former riverbed), 320 sunny days, and rent that hasn't gone fully insane yet. Has become the default 'Barcelona but cheaper' for many remote workers.
valencia.weather: Mediterranean — very warm but less humid than Barcelona, mild winters
valencia.best_neighborhoods: Ruzafa (hip, central), El Carmen (old town), Cabanyal (beach), Benimaclet (student-y, cheap)
valencia.expat_density: rapidly growing — strong digital nomad scene since 2022
valencia.pros: huge bang-for-buck, less tourist-saturated than BCN, paella was literally invented here, easy day-trips
valencia.cons: limited international flight options vs Madrid/BCN, July–August is genuinely too hot, smaller English-speaking professional network

granada.name: Granada
granada.blurb: The Alhambra, free tapas with every drink, and rent that still feels like 2015. Smaller (~230k) so the expat scene is more concentrated. Sierra Nevada an hour away for skiing; Costa Tropical an hour the other way for beach. Punches above its weight on quality of life.
granada.weather: high-altitude continental — 4 real seasons (rare in Spain), hot dry summers (35°C+), cold winters with occasional snow
granada.best_neighborhoods: Realejo (historic, central), Albaicín (UNESCO, hilly, photogenic), Centro (walkable, restaurants), Zaidín (cheaper, residential)
granada.pros: free tapas with every drink (genuinely), low cost-of-living, walkable, ski + beach within 1h, university town energy
granada.cons: small city = small professional network, limited international flights, summer heat is brutal, slower pace if you came from a metro

bilbao.name: Bilbao
bilbao.blurb: Basque Country anchor city. Reinvented itself from industrial port to design capital after the Guggenheim. Strong Basque cultural identity (Euskara is a separate language; Spanish works fine). Rains more than the rest of Spain — locals call it 'sirimiri' weather.
bilbao.weather: Atlantic — mild, wet year-round (similar to Pacific Northwest), summers 22–26°C, winters 8–12°C
bilbao.best_neighborhoods: Casco Viejo (old town, lively), Indautxu (residential, central), Deusto (across the river, university), Getxo (suburb, beach)
bilbao.pros: world-class food scene (Michelin density), strong economy + tech jobs, 30 min from beaches and surf, distinct culture
bilbao.cons: wettest weather in Spain, Basque cultural friction (some), smaller English-speaking network, more expensive than Andalusia

sansebastian.name: San Sebastián
sansebastian.blurb: Smaller cousin to Bilbao on the same Atlantic coast. Two perfect beaches inside the city, 19 Michelin stars in a town of 187k, and pintxos culture that makes 'going out for tapas' feel embarrassing in comparison. Expensive by Spanish standards.
sansebastian.weather: Atlantic — milder than Bilbao but still wet, summers 20–25°C, winters 8–12°C
sansebastian.best_neighborhoods: Centro (touristy, expensive), Gros (surfer/local mix, beach), Antiguo (residential, near Igeldo), Egia (artsy, cheaper)
sansebastian.expat_density: moderate, lots of international foodies + remote workers post-2020
sansebastian.pros: stunning natural setting, world's densest concentration of great food, 1h to French border, walkable everywhere
sansebastian.cons: expensive (one of Spain's priciest cities), wet weather, very seasonal tourism in summer, hard rental market

portugal.name: Portugal
portugal.tax_perk: NHR closed — IFICI is the narrow replacement

lisbon.name: Lisbon
lisbon.blurb: Hills, tile, light, and the most expensive housing in Portugal by a wide margin. Strong English fluency, big startup ecosystem, big American influx since 2020. Locals have feelings about the Americans.
lisbon.weather: Atlantic Mediterranean — mild year-round, occasional rain Oct–Mar, summers 25–30°C
lisbon.best_neighborhoods: Príncipe Real (central, expensive), Estrela (residential), Marvila (up-and-coming, ex-industrial), Cascais (coastal, 30min train)
lisbon.expat_density: very high — largest American expat community in Portugal
lisbon.pros: highest English fluency in Iberia, lowest D7 income threshold in EU, dual citizenship allowed, citizenship in 5 years
lisbon.cons: rent rose 60%+ since 2020, AIMA appointment backlogs are real, hills are steep, summer water shortages

porto.name: Porto
porto.blurb: Smaller, grittier, cheaper, and arguably more characterful than Lisbon. Port wine country. Slower pace, denser Portuguese culture, less expat saturation. The river district (Ribeira) is touristy; the rest is daily life.
porto.weather: Atlantic — wetter than Lisbon, milder summers (22–26°C), gray winters
porto.best_neighborhoods: Bonfim (residential, central), Cedofeita (artsy), Foz (coastal upscale), Vila Nova de Gaia (across the river, cheaper)
porto.pros: 20-30% cheaper than Lisbon, walkable, real Portuguese cultural fabric, port wine cellars on demand
porto.cons: limited international flights, weather is the wettest of the Iberian options, smaller startup scene

faro.name: Faro
faro.blurb: Algarve hub. Small, sun-drenched, with the best weather in continental Europe. The international airport makes it more connected than its size suggests. Strong UK and German retiree presence; growing American.
faro.weather: subtropical Mediterranean — driest area of Portugal, 300+ sunny days, mild winters (15–18°C)
faro.best_neighborhoods: Faro old town (historic), Montenegro (suburb, family-oriented), nearby Olhão and Tavira (smaller, cheaper)
faro.pros: best year-round weather in Portugal, beach access, lower cost than Lisbon/Porto, English widely spoken (UK retiree influence)
faro.cons: small, can feel quiet outside summer, fewer professional networking options, tourism-driven economy seasonality

cascais.name: Cascais
cascais.blurb: Coastal town 30 min by train from Lisbon. Premium prices, beach access, ex-fishing-village vibes overrun by international wealth. Where well-off Lisbon-area expats settle when they're tired of city density. Tighter community than the Lisbon center.
cascais.weather: Atlantic Mediterranean — milder than Lisbon, breezy, less stifling in August
cascais.best_neighborhoods: Centro (walkable, expensive), Estoril (next-town-over, still pricey), Birre (residential, family-oriented), Quinta da Marinha (gated, golf-adjacent)
cascais.expat_density: very high — significant American + Northern European retiree/remote-worker population
cascais.pros: beach + ocean breeze + Lisbon access in one package, English everywhere, large established expat community, family-friendly schools
cascais.cons: expensive (rivaling Lisbon centre), summer is genuinely overrun with tourists, train is the only realistic non-car commute

mexico.name: Mexico
mexico.tax_perk: no special regime (worldwide income taxed for residents)

mexico_city.name: Mexico City (CDMX)
mexico_city.blurb: 21 million people, an altitude that surprises everyone (2,240m), and a food scene that justifies the move on its own. Strong Roma/Condesa expat clusters with a heated debate about gentrification. Chilango weather: spring all year.
mexico_city.transport_pass: Metro is 5 pesos/ride (~$0.30), no monthly pass
mexico_city.weather: high-altitude temperate — 18–25°C year-round, rainy season May–Oct, dry Nov–Apr
mexico_city.best_neighborhoods: Roma Norte (cafés, nomads, expensive), Condesa (parks, bars), Polanco (upscale), Coyoacán (historic, Frida Kahlo's old turf)
mexico_city.expat_density: very high — biggest American expat community in Mexico
mexico_city.pros: world-class food at low prices, huge cultural offering, no FBI check needed for visa, fast resident card processing
mexico_city.cons: altitude affects newcomers for ~2 weeks, traffic is genuinely apocalyptic, air quality drops Nov–Feb, water purity precautions needed

playa_del_carmen.name: Playa del Carmen
playa_del_carmen.blurb: Caribbean beach town that grew up. Strong digital nomad infrastructure: coworking on every block, English-speaking everything, USD-pegged prices in the touristy zones. Trade-off: less Mexican, more international beach town.
playa_del_carmen.weather: tropical — warm year-round (25–32°C), hurricane season Jun–Nov, very humid
playa_del_carmen.best_neighborhoods: Playacar (gated, expat-heavy), Centro (walkable, touristy), Colonia Ejidal (more local, cheaper)
playa_del_carmen.pros: Caribbean beach 5-min walk from anywhere, large nomad community, no FBI check, easy visa, USD widely accepted
playa_del_carmen.cons: tourist pricing, sargassum (seaweed) season can be rough, hurricane risk Jun–Nov, water/electrical infrastructure inconsistent

san_miguel.name: San Miguel de Allende
san_miguel.blurb: Colonial UNESCO town turned American expat capital. Different demographic from CDMX/Playa: skews older (retirees), wealthier, more culturally American-in-Mexico than Mexican. Beautiful, walkable, and increasingly expensive.
san_miguel.weather: high-altitude temperate (1,900m) — sunny year-round, cool nights, dry climate
san_miguel.best_neighborhoods: Centro (historic, expensive, walkable), San Antonio (residential, cheaper), Los Frailes (suburban, gated communities)
san_miguel.expat_density: extremely high — one of the densest American expat populations in Latin America
san_miguel.pros: extraordinary architecture, year-round perfect weather, English everywhere, large established expat community with services
san_miguel.cons: expensive by Mexican standards, can feel like an American bubble, limited career networking, prices have risen sharply since 2020

oaxaca.name: Oaxaca
oaxaca.blurb: Cultural capital of southern Mexico. Indigenous Zapotec roots, mezcal valley below the city, food scene that justifies a flight on its own. Less expat-saturated than San Miguel but rapidly catching up — locals are watching the gentrification carefully.
oaxaca.weather: high-altitude temperate (1,550m) — perfect spring weather year-round, brief rainy season May–Sep
oaxaca.best_neighborhoods: Centro (historic, walkable), Reforma (residential, cheaper, central), Jalatlaco (artsy, restaurants), Xochimilco (quiet, traditional)
oaxaca.pros: best food in Mexico (debate me), low cost-of-living, walkable, deep cultural offerings, relatively safe
oaxaca.cons: limited international flight options, gentrification tension is real, smaller English-speaking professional network than CDMX, infrastructure inconsistent outside centro

tulum.name: Tulum
tulum.blurb: Caribbean coast, jungle, cenotes, and a real-estate boom that has run completely off the rails since 2020. The town that 'spiritual entrepreneurs' on Instagram fled to. Great for a 90-day digital-nomad stint; harder as a long-term base because infrastructure hasn't kept up.
tulum.internet: 30–50 USD (fiber spotty, often via Starlink for reliability)
tulum.weather: tropical — warm year-round (26–32°C), hurricane season Jun–Nov, very humid, sargassum season Apr–Sep
tulum.best_neighborhoods: Centro (walkable, more local-priced), La Veleta (residential, family-friendly), Aldea Zama (gated, expat-heavy), Beach zone (resorts + restaurants, very expensive)
tulum.pros: unbelievable nature (cenotes, beaches, ruins), large international wellness/nomad community, easy 90-day visa entry, no FBI check needed for residency
tulum.cons: infrastructure (electric, water, internet) is the weakest of all options here, prices are USD-pegged and tourist-inflated, hurricane risk, sargassum can ruin beaches
